unit: MW of IT load per MW of facility power drawn (= 1/PUE) at the industry-average PUE
source: Uptime Institute, Global Data Center Survey 2025 (keynote report PDF, survey run Apr-May 2025)
note: 1 / 1.54 = 0.649, so a 100 MW grid connection at the industry-average PUE supports about 65 MW of IT load; use this for older or colocation halls, not for new hyperscale AI builds.

unit: kW of IT load per liquid-cooled GB200 NVL72 rack
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, NVIDIA Contributes NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 Designs to Open Compute Project (15 Oct 2024)
note: Design figure; 1 MW of IT load supports about 8 such racks (1,000 / 120 = 8.3); Microsoft reports ~140 kW per rack in production for GB200/GB300, which gives about 7 racks per MW.

unit: liters of on-site water consumed per kWh of data-center electricity (WUE, US average)
source: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (Dec 2024)
note: LBNL modelled US average site WUE through 2023; a 100 MW facility at PUE 1.3 and 0.36 L/kWh would consume about 100,000 kW x 1.3 x 8,760 h x 0.36 L = 410 million liters a year; AWS reports a fleet WUE of 0.15 L/kWh and closed-loop designs (Microsoft Fairwater, Crusoe Abilene) approach zero evaporation; indirect water via power generation is far larger at 4.52 L/kWh.

unit: accredited MW per nameplate MW (PJM ELCC, gas combined cycle, 2027/28)
source: PJM, ELCC Class Ratings for the 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction
note: The quoted row is the table's values in reading order for these classes: Onshore Wind 41%, Offshore Wind 67%, Fixed-Tilt Solar 7%, Tracking Solar 8%, Landfill 48%, Hydro Intermittent 39%, 4-hr Storage 58%, 6-hr 67%, 8-hr 70%, 10-hr 78%, Demand Resource 92%, Nuclear 95%, Coal 83%, Gas Combined Cycle 74%, Gas Combustion Turbine 61%, Gas CT Dual Fuel 77%, Diesel 92%, Steam 72%, Waste to Energy 83%, Oil-Fired CT 80%; a 1,000 MW combined-cycle plant therefore counts 740 MW toward PJM's reliability requirement and a nuclear unit 950 MW.

unit: Btu of natural gas per kWh generated (heat rate, new combined-cycle, upper bound)
source: EIA, Today in Energy: Use of natural gas-fired generation differs in the United States by technology and region (February 22, 2024)
note: 7,000 Btu/kWh equals 7.0 MMBtu per MWh (7,000 x 1,000 / 1,000,000); a 1 GW combined-cycle plant at full output burns 7,000 MMBtu per hour or 168,000 MMBtu per day, about 0.16 Bcf/d at 1,037 Btu per cubic foot (168,000,000,000 / 1,037 = 162 million cf), so 10 GW of new gas plants for data centres is roughly 1.6 Bcf/d of gas demand; simple-cycle turbines run above 10,000 Btu/kWh.

unit: GW of active interconnection-queue capacity per GW of installed US generating capacity (end-2025)
source: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Queued Up: 2026 Edition (June 2026)
note: 2,061 / 1,374 = 1.50 (my arithmetic); LBNL's 1,374 GW installed figure is higher than EIA's 1,280,799 MW of utility-scale capacity at end-2025 (likely a nameplate versus net-summer or coverage difference), so the ratio is 1.5-1.6 depending on the denominator; with 13% historical completion the queue implies perhaps 270 GW of eventual builds (2,061 x 0.13).

unit: MW of IT load per MW of facility power drawn (= 1/PUE) at Google's fleet PUE
source: Google Data Centers, Power usage effectiveness (efficiency page)
note: 1 / 1.09 = 0.917, so a 100 MW connection supports about 92 MW of IT at best-in-class efficiency; new liquid-cooled AI campuses (Microsoft Fairwater, Crusoe Abilene) are designed toward this end of the range.

unit: USD million of construction cost per MW of capacity (shell, power and cooling; excludes IT)
source: JLL Research, 2026 Global Data Center Outlook (5 Jan 2026)
note: Global average for 2025; US markets range from $9.5/W (Charlotte) to $13.3/W (Silicon Valley) in Turner & Townsend's index, i.e. $9.5M-$13.3M per MW, with a 7-10% premium for AI-ready liquid-cooled halls; a 1 GW campus is therefore roughly $10-13B before any GPUs.

unit: GPUs per GB200 NVL72 rack
source: NVIDIA, GB200 NVL72 product page
note: 72 Blackwell GPUs plus 36 Grace CPUs per rack; at 120 kW per rack that is 120 / 72 = 1.67 kW per GPU at the rack (including CPUs, NVLink switches and fans but excluding facility cooling and power losses, which the PUE factor adds).

unit: Blackwell GPUs per MW of campus IT load, all-in (compute, storage, networking)
source: Epoch AI, AI Data Centers directory (estimates; page updated 24 Sep 2026)
note: Arithmetic from Epoch's Abilene estimate: 100.8k B200 + 100.8k B300 = 201,600 GPUs / 421 MW IT = 479 GPUs per MW, i.e. 2.09 kW of IT load per GPU; Epoch's Colossus 2 figures give a similar 440,000 / 946 = 465 per MW; SemiAnalysis counted ~110k GB200 for ~200 MW at Colossus 2 (550 per MW); these are tracker estimates, not operator disclosures.

unit: acres of campus land per MW of capacity (Vantage Frontier design)
source: Vantage Data Centers press release, Vantage Data Centers Unveils Plans for Frontier, a $25B Mega-campus in Texas (19 Aug 2025)
note: Arithmetic: 1,200 acres / 1,400 MW = 0.86 acres per MW, with 3.7 million sq ft of buildings for 1.4 GW (2,640 sq ft per MW); Meta Hyperion is nearly 10 million sq ft for 5 GW (2,000 sq ft per MW); land is rarely the binding constraint, power and permits are.

unit: accredited MW per nameplate MW (PJM ELCC, tracking solar, 2027/28)
source: PJM, ELCC Class Ratings for the 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction
note: Tracking solar is accredited at 8% and 4-hour storage at 58% of nameplate, so the 43.4 GW of solar and 24 GW of batteries planned nationally for 2026 would count for only about 3.5 GW and 13.9 GW of firm capacity under PJM's method (43.4 x 0.08; 24 x 0.58, my arithmetic, applied to a national figure for illustration).

unit: capacity factor (MWh generated per MW-hour of capacity, newest US combined-cycle fleet, 2022)
source: EIA, Today in Energy: Use of natural gas-fired generation differs in the United States by technology and region (February 22, 2024)
note: 1 MW of new combined-cycle capacity produced about 5,782 MWh per year at this rate (0.66 x 8,760 h, my arithmetic); the whole CCGT fleet averaged about 56% in 2022, and a data centre running near 100% load needs firm capacity sized well above its average draw.

unit: $ per kW-year of accredited capacity (PJM 2027/28 capacity price converted from $/MW-day)
source: PJM Inside Lines, PJM Auction Procures 134,479 MW of Generation Resources (December 17, 2025)
note: $333.44 per MW-day x 365 days / 1,000 kW per MW = $121.71 per kW-year (my arithmetic); this is what a 100 MW data centre's share of PJM capacity costs, about $12.2 million a year before the ELCC and load-forecast adjustments, and it is the price signal that new firm generation earns on top of energy revenue.

unit: MW of IT load per MW of facility power (1 / PUE, global weighted-average PUE 1.54)
source: Uptime Institute, Global Data Center Survey 2025 (Keynote Report 180, July 2025)
note: 1 / 1.54 = 0.649 (my arithmetic): a data centre drawing 100 MW at the grid connection supports about 65 MW of servers and networking at the industry-average PUE; the figure has barely moved for six years.

unit: MW of IT load per MW of facility power (1 / PUE, data centres of 20 MW and above, PUE 1.44)
source: Uptime Institute, Global Data Center Survey 2025 (Keynote Report 180, July 2025)
note: 1 / 1.44 = 0.694 (my arithmetic); large, newer facilities of the kind hyperscalers build are more efficient, so a 1 GW grid connection yields roughly 690 MW of IT load rather than 650 MW; facilities commissioned since about 2020 average PUE 1.48.

unit: kW per rack (average of modal rack densities, 2025 survey)
source: Uptime Institute, Global Data Center Survey 2025 (Keynote Report 180, July 2025)
note: Typical rack density across all surveyed data centres, so 1 MW of IT load is about 111 conventional racks (1,000 / 9, my arithmetic); AI racks are far denser (an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack is rated around 120 kW), which is why AI halls need liquid cooling and far more power per square foot.

unit: GB of HBM per GPU (NVIDIA H100 SXM, HBM3)
source: NVIDIA, H100 Tensor Core GPU product page specification table
note: H100 SXM lists 80GB of HBM3 at 3.35TB/s; the PCIe-based H100 NVL variant lists 94GB.

unit: HBM stacks per GPU (NVIDIA H100 SXM5, active HBM3 stacks)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'NVIDIA Hopper Architecture In-Depth', March 22, 2022
note: Five active 16 GB HBM3 stacks give 80 GB; the package has six stack sites, one left unused for yield.

unit: GB of HBM per GPU (NVIDIA H200 SXM and H200 NVL, HBM3e)
source: NVIDIA, H200 Tensor Core GPU product page and specification table
note: Per-GPU HBM3e capacity from NVIDIA's own specification table (4.8TB/s); same GPU die as H100 with six 24 GB stacks, of which 141 GB is exposed.

unit: GB of HBM3e per GPU as configured in DGX B200 (1,440 GB / 8 GPUs)
source: NVIDIA, DGX B200 product page specification table
note: Arithmetic: 1,440 GB total across 8x Blackwell GPUs = 180 GB per GPU as shipped; the Blackwell GPU's full on-package capacity is 192 GB (next row).

unit: GB of HBM3e per GPU (NVIDIA Blackwell B200, on-package capacity)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'Inside NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra', Aug 22, 2025
note: Derived: Blackwell Ultra's 288 GB is stated to be 50% more than Blackwell, so 288 / 1.5 = 192 GB for Blackwell, i.e. eight 8-Hi stacks of 24 GB.

unit: GB of HBM3e per GPU (NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra / GB300)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'Inside NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra', Aug 22, 2025
note: Per-GPU HBM3e capacity for the GB300 generation; a GB300 NVL72 rack lists 72 GPUs and 20 TB of GPU memory (72 x 288 GB = 20,736 GB).

unit: HBM stacks per GPU (NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra, 12-Hi HBM3e stacks of 36 GB)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'Inside NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra', Aug 22, 2025
note: Eight stacks x 12 dies x 3 GB = 288 GB; stack count per GPU has gone 5 (H100) to 6 (H200) to 8 (B200 and GB300), and dies per stack from 8 to 12.

unit: DRAM wafers consumed per bit, HBM3E relative to DDR5 at the same node (ratio)
source: MLQ News report of Micron's Hot Chips 2026 presentation (Raghu Sreeramaneni, Micron), Aug 26, 2026
note: Micron's 'trade ratio': each HBM bit removes about three DDR5 bits of wafer capacity, and Micron said the HBM4 ratio is higher. Secondary report of a company presentation; Micron's own remarks PDFs redirect.

unit: GPUs per GB300 NVL72 rack, with 20 TB of GPU memory per rack
source: NVIDIA, GB300 NVL72 product page specification table
note: The page lists 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 20 TB of GPU memory per rack; 72 x 288 GB = 20.7 TB, so '20 TB' is a rounded rack total.

unit: teraFLOPS FP8 Tensor Core per GPU, with sparsity (H100 SXM)
source: NVIDIA, H100 Tensor Core GPU product page, specifications table
note: Hopper-generation peak FP8 throughput per GPU as listed in the datasheet table; the figure is 'with sparsity', so dense FP8 is half (1,979 teraFLOPS), and FP16/BF16 with sparsity is 1,979 teraFLOPS. The quote is a table cell, hence shorter than eight words.

unit: petaFLOPS FP8 Tensor Core per GPU, with sparsity (B200, from 72 PFLOPS per 8-GPU DGX B200)
source: NVIDIA, DGX B200 product page, specifications table
note: Arithmetic: DGX B200 lists FP8 Tensor Core 72 PFLOPS for 8 Blackwell GPUs, so 72 / 8 = 9 PFLOPS per B200, about 2.3x the H100's 3.958 PFLOPS; the GB200 NVL72 page lists FP4 1,440 PFLOPS for 72 GPUs, i.e. 20 PFLOPS FP4 per GB200 GPU. The quote is a table cell.

unit: kW per GPU, chip TDP only (H100 SXM)
source: NVIDIA, H100 Tensor Core GPU product page, specifications table
note: Arithmetic: 700 W = 0.7 kW; this is the GPU module's maximum thermal design power alone, before CPUs, networking, fans and cooling overhead. The PCIe/NVL variant is 350-400 W.

unit: kW per GPU, chip TDP only (Blackwell GPU in the GB200 superchip)
source: Wccftech, NVIDIA's Fully-Enabled Blackwell B200 GPUs Consume Up To 1200W (Mar. 22, 2024), reporting NVIDIA GTC 2024 sessions
note: Arithmetic: 1,200 W = 1.2 kW for the full-spec Blackwell GPU used in GB200; the same report says the HGX/DGX B200 variant 'is optimized around 1000W' (1.0 kW) and B100 at 700 W. NVIDIA's own GB200 NVL72 page lists no power figure, so this is a press report of NVIDIA engineers' statements rather than a datasheet.

unit: kW per GPU, all-in at the server level (DGX B200, 8 GPUs)
source: NVIDIA, DGX B200 product page, specifications table
note: Arithmetic: the 8-GPU DGX B200 system draws about 14.3 kW maximum, so 14.3 / 8 = 1.79 kW per GPU including the two host CPUs, NICs, fans and power-supply losses; this is the number to use for IT load per GPU in an air-cooled Blackwell server, versus about 1.0 kW for the GPU chip alone.

unit: kW of IT load per GB200 NVL72 rack (72 GPUs), liquid-cooled
source: SemiAnalysis, GB200 Hardware Architecture - Component Supply Chain & BOM (July 17, 2024), free section
note: Rack-level power for the 72-GPU NVL72 (18 compute trays at a 6.3 kW max TDP each plus NVLink switch trays); arithmetic: 120 / 72 = 1.67 kW per GPU all-in, and a hosting provider (Pantheon, Aug. 2026) says NVIDIA's rack guide lists approximately 120 kW for GB200 NVL72 and up to 142 kW for GB300 NVL72. Requires direct liquid cooling; typical air-cooled H100 racks were about 40 kW.

unit: GPUs per rack (GB200 NVL72)
source: NVIDIA, GB200 NVL72 product page, specifications table
note: One NVL72 rack holds 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs in a single NVLink domain; the same table lists 13.4 TB of HBM3E per rack, i.e. 13,400 / 72 = 186 GB of HBM per GPU (or 372 GB per two-GPU superchip), which is the bridge to the memory stage.

unit: gross CoWoS interposers (GPU packages) per 300 mm wafer, before yield (low end of 25-28)
source: Silicon Analysts, CoWoS Cost 2026: $750-1,100/Chip, Chiplet vs Monolithic (Apr. 13, 2026)
note: Analyst-site estimate with no primary citation, for a B200-class package (two near-reticle dies plus eight HBM stacks); applying its 60-70% interposer yield gives about 15-19 good packages per CoWoS wafer, so 130,000 wafers per month would be roughly 2-2.5 million such GPUs per month. TSMC does not publish packages per wafer; treat as an order-of-magnitude figure.

unit: GPUs per NVL72 rack
source: NVIDIA, GB200 NVL72 product page (specifications table)
note: One GB200 or GB300 NVL72 rack holds 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs across 18 compute trays (4 GPUs + 2 CPUs each) plus 9 NVLink switch trays; a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack keeps the same 72-GPU count.

unit: GPUs per HGX/DGX 8-GPU server
source: NVIDIA, DGX B200 product page (specifications table)
note: The HGX baseboard design used by every OEM 8-GPU server (Supermicro, Dell XE9680, HPE, etc.) carries eight GPUs; a DGX B200 occupies 10 rack units, so air-cooled racks typically hold 2 to 4 such servers (16 to 32 GPUs) against 72 in a liquid-cooled NVL72.

unit: kW per GPU at the rack (NVL72, rated rack power incl. CPUs, NVLink switches, in-rack CDU)
source: Supermicro, 'Supermicro NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 Datasheet' (PDF), rack specifications table
note: Arithmetic: 132 kW rated rack power / 72 GPUs = 1.833 kW per GPU; using the datasheet's operating range of 125-135 kW gives 1.74-1.88 kW per GPU. Excludes scale-out network switches, storage and facility cooling overhead (PUE), which belong to the datacenter stage.

unit: kW per GPU at the server (HGX/DGX B200 8-GPU, max system power incl. CPUs and NICs)
source: NVIDIA, DGX B200 product page (specifications table)
note: Arithmetic: 14.3 kW max system power / 8 GPUs = 1.79 kW per GPU, including the two CPUs, memory, storage and ConnectX-7/BlueField-3 NICs inside the server but not the external switches; per GPU this is close to the NVL72 figure despite the NVL72's far higher density per rack.

unit: GB of HBM3E per GPU (GB200)
source: NVIDIA, GB200 NVL72 product page (specifications table)
note: Arithmetic: 13.4 TB of HBM3E per rack / 72 GPUs = 0.186 TB = 186 GB per GPU (from NVIDIA's rounded rack total; each Blackwell GPU carries 8 HBM3E stacks, so about 23 GB per stack).

unit: GB of HBM3e per GPU (GB300 / Blackwell Ultra)
source: NVIDIA, GB300 NVL72 product page (specifications table)
note: Arithmetic: 20 TB of GPU memory per GB300 NVL72 rack / 72 GPUs = 0.278 TB = 278 GB per GPU, a 49% increase in HBM per GPU over GB200 for the same 72-GPU rack, which is why HBM demand grows faster than GPU unit counts.

unit: USD per GPU deployed in an 8-GPU HGX B200 server (system-level price, all components)
source: Mercatus AI blog, 'NVIDIA B200 Server Price in 2026: What an 8-GPU HGX System Costs' (16 Jul 2026)
note: Arithmetic check: a typical $450,000 server / 8 GPUs = $56,250 per GPU, versus a bare B200 card list price of $30,000-40,000, so the server wrapper (CPUs, memory, NICs, storage, chassis, integrator margin) adds roughly 40-90% on top of the GPU; the $2.8-3.4 million GB200 NVL72 estimate implies $38,900-47,200 per GPU at rack level. Reseller compilation, not a filing.

unit: USD of API tokens per developer per active day, Claude Code enterprise average
source: Anthropic, Claude Code documentation, 'Manage costs effectively' (accessed 27 Sep 2026)
note: Anthropic's own average for enterprise deployments billed per token, with 90 percent of users under $30 per active day and $150-250 per developer per month. Illustrative tokens (model mix is not published): at Sonnet 5 list prices of $2 per million input and $10 per million output (claude.com/pricing), $13 buys 1.3 million output tokens or 6.5 million uncached input tokens, so a typical coding seat is in the low millions of tokens per active day, the heavy-tier band in consumption_tiers.csv.

unit: USD per Agentforce agent action (list, via Flex Credits)
source: Salesforce, 'Agentforce Pricing' page (accessed 27 Sep 2026)
note: Arithmetic: Flex Credits cost '$500 USD/Per 100k Credits' = $0.005 per credit; an Agentforce action consumes 20 credits, so 20 x $0.005 = $0.10 per action (voice actions are 30 credits = $0.15). Together with $2 per conversation this is the public price of a unit of enterprise agent work, which the 3.2 billion Agentic Work Units per quarter can be multiplied against.

unit: USD per second of generated video, Runway Gen-4.5 on the Standard plan
source: Runway, 'Pricing' page (accessed 27 Sep 2026)
note: Arithmetic: Standard plan $12 per month for 625 credits = $0.0192 per credit; Gen-4.5 burns 12 credits per second, so 12 x $0.0192 = $0.2304 per second (about 52 seconds of video per month). On the Max plan ($76 for 9,500 credits, $0.008 per credit) the same second costs $0.096. This is what a consumer pays; the compute cost behind it is not disclosed.

unit: USD per second of generated video with audio, Google Veo 3.1 Standard (720p and 1080p), API list price
source: Google AI for Developers, 'Gemini Developer API Pricing' page, Veo 3.1 section (accessed 27 Sep 2026)
note: Per-second API price for the standard Veo 3.1 video model; the same table lists Veo 3.1 Fast at $0.10 per second (720p) and $0.60 per second for 4K standard output. Arithmetic: an 8-second clip costs 8 x $0.40 = $3.20 at standard quality, versus about 8 x $0.2304 = $1.84 on Runway's Standard plan. The quote is the table cell for the standard 720p/1080p rate; the page's row label is 'Veo 3.1 Standard video with audio price (default)'.

unit: tokens per year that define a 'trillion-token' Azure Foundry enterprise customer
source: Microsoft FY26 Q4 earnings call, 29 Jul 2026, Satya Nadella remarks (transcript hosted by StockAnalysis)
note: A threshold Microsoft uses to count its largest API customers, not an average; arithmetic: 1e12 / 365 = about 2.7 billion tokens per day per such customer, or roughly 2,700 heavy-tier developers at 1 million tokens a day each. On the FY26 Q3 call Microsoft put the count at over 300 customers on track for the year. Third-party transcript, so quote accuracy depends on the transcriber.

unit: Wh per average ChatGPT query
source: Sam Altman (OpenAI CEO) personal blog, 'The Gentle Singularity' (June 2025; the page shows no date)
note: The only OpenAI-attributed energy-per-query figure; no methodology is published and 'average query' is undefined, so treat as an order of magnitude. Arithmetic: 0.34 Wh x 1,000,000 queries = 340 kWh per million queries; at 900 million weekly users making one query a day each, 0.34 Wh x 900e6 = 306 MWh per day, about 12.8 MW of continuous load.

unit: Wh per median Gemini Apps text prompt
source: Google Cloud blog, 'Measuring the environmental impact of AI inference' (21 Aug 2025)
note: Google's own full-stack measurement (accelerators, host CPU and DRAM, idle capacity and data-centre overhead) for the median text prompt in the Gemini app in May 2025; a median, not a mean, so heavy prompts, image and video generation and agentic use are not represented. Arithmetic: 0.24 Wh x 1,000,000 prompts = 240 kWh per million prompts.

unit: kW of rack IT load per GPU (GB200 NVL72: 120 kW rack / 72 GPUs)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'NVIDIA Contributes NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 Designs to Open Compute Project' (15 Oct 2024)
note: Arithmetic: 120 kW / 72 GPUs = 1.667 kW per GPU at the rack (GPU, Grace CPU, NVLink switches, in-rack cooling). Excludes scale-out network, storage and facility overhead (PUE), which the datacenter stage adds.

unit: kW of system power per GPU (DGX H100: 10.2 kW max / 8 GPUs)
source: NVIDIA DGX H100/H200 User Guide, 'Introduction to the NVIDIA DGX H100/H200 Systems', hardware specifications
note: Arithmetic: 10.2 kW / 8 GPUs = 1.275 kW per GPU for an air-cooled H100 server at maximum system power ('10.2 kW max.' on the same spec table; H100 SXM TDP is up to 700 W, so the server roughly doubles the GPU's own draw). Excludes network switches and facility overhead.

unit: GPU-hours per MW-year of rack IT load (GB200 density, 100% uptime)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'NVIDIA Contributes NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 Designs to Open Compute Project' (15 Oct 2024); arithmetic by this note
note: Arithmetic: 1,000 kW / 1.667 kW per GPU = 600 GPUs per MW of rack IT load; 600 x 8,760 hours = 5,256,000 GPU-hours per MW-year if every GPU is rentable every hour. Sellable hours are lower by utilisation (Oracle reported 97.9%) and by facility overhead: at PUE 1.2 the figure per MW of facility power is 4,380,000. At H100 density (1.275 kW per GPU) it is 784 GPUs and 6,870,588 GPU-hours per MW-year.

unit: USD m of revenue per MW-year of rack IT load at $6.52 per GPU-hour (B200 on-demand median, GB200 density, 100% utilisation)
source: AIMultiple, 'Cloud GPU Rental Price Index' (Sep 2026) for the price; NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 blog for the density; arithmetic by this note
note: Arithmetic: 5,256,000 GPU-hours per MW-year x $6.52 = $34.27 million per MW-year, a ceiling using on-demand list prices at full utilisation. At H100 density and the $3.25 H100 median: 6,870,588 x $3.25 = $22.33 million. Contract-level cross-checks are lower: Nebius cites $20-25 million per MW of annual contract value and Together AI/HUMAIN expect over $5 billion on 250 MW (= $20 million per MW-year).

unit: USD m of annual contract value per MW (low end of Nebius' $20-25 million range on recent large deals)
source: Nebius Group N.V., Form 6-K Exhibit 99.2, Letter to shareholders Q2 2026 (12 Aug 2026)
note: A company-stated contract yield per megawatt for multi-year GPU capacity deals, the best public anchor for 'revenue per MW-year on contract'. Implied contract price: $20-25 million / 5,256,000 GPU-hours (GB200 density) = $3.81-4.76 per GPU-hour, below the $6.52 B200 on-demand median. High end 25.

unit: USD m of lease revenue per MW-year paid by a GPU cloud to its data-centre landlord (Applied Digital portfolio)
source: Applied Digital Corporation, Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026; arithmetic by this note
note: Arithmetic: $36.2 billion / 1,410 MW / 15 years = $1.71 million per MW-year. The landlord's take is under a tenth of the $20-25 million per MW-year a GPU cloud books on the same megawatt, which shows where the margin (and the GPU capex) sits.

unit: output tokens per second per GPU (Llama 3.3 70B, NVIDIA B200, NVFP4, at 50 tokens/s per user, InferenceMAX 1K/1K)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'NVIDIA Blackwell Leads on New SemiAnalysis InferenceMAX Benchmarks' (13 Oct 2025)
note: Vendor-run result on SemiAnalysis's open InferenceMAX suite for a 70B dense model at moderate interactivity: 10,000 tokens/s per GPU = 36 million tokens per GPU-hour (10,000 x 3,600); NVIDIA says this is more than 4x the H200, implying roughly 2,500 tokens/s per H200. Throughput falls steeply as per-user speed rises (for DeepSeek-R1 on B200 SemiAnalysis shows about 4,800 tokens/s/GPU at 42 tokens/s per user but about 500 at 100), so any single figure must carry its interactivity target.

unit: output tokens per second per GPU (DeepSeek-R1 671B, FP4, 8x Blackwell B200 DGX, max-throughput mode)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'NVIDIA Blackwell Delivers World-Record DeepSeek-R1 Inference Performance' (18 Mar 2025)
note: Arithmetic: 30,000 tokens/s per 8-GPU DGX B200 / 8 GPUs = 3,750 tokens/s per GPU, or 13.5 million tokens per GPU-hour, for a 671B-parameter mixture-of-experts reasoning model at low interactivity; the same system serves over 250 tokens/s to one user when tuned for latency instead. Vendor benchmark at FP4, so an upper bound for production serving.

unit: USD of rented GPU time per 1M output tokens (B200 at Lambda on-demand $6.69/GPU-hr, Llama 3.3 70B at 10,000 tokens/s per GPU)
source: Lambda, 'GPU cloud pricing: rent NVIDIA H100, H200, and B200' (on-demand instances table, as fetched 27 Sep 2026)
note: Arithmetic: 10,000 tokens/s x 3,600 s = 36,000,000 tokens per GPU-hour; $6.69 / 36 = $0.186 per 1M output tokens for GPU rental alone, before margin, idle time, input-token processing and the lower utilisation of real traffic. Against list prices of $3.96 (DeepSeek), $6 (Grok 4.7), $12 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and $50 (gpt-6-astra, Claude Fable 5.1) per 1M output tokens, the raw GPU cost is a small fraction of the price of a frontier closed model but a large fraction of an open-weight one. Quote is the table text; the header column is PRICE/GPU/HR.

unit: USD per 1M output tokens (DeepSeek-R1 on GB200 NVL72 at about 75 tokens/s per user; NVIDIA's own cost model)
source: NVIDIA Technical Blog, 'NVIDIA Blackwell Leads on New SemiAnalysis InferenceMAX Benchmarks' (13 Oct 2025)
note: NVIDIA's stated cost per million tokens using InferenceMAX throughput and its own GPU-hour cost assumptions (not disclosed on the page): $1.56 on H200 versus just over $0.10 on GB200 NVL72 for DeepSeek-R1 at about 75 tokens/s per user, a 15x gap; for gpt-oss-120b at 100 tokens/s per user it fell from $0.11 to $0.02 in two months of software updates. Shows how fast serving cost moves with hardware generation and software, independent of list prices.

unit: FLOP of training compute per parameter per training token (the 6ND rule)
source: Epoch AI, 'Data on AI models: documentation, estimation methods' (page as fetched 27 Sep 2026)
note: Standard heuristic for dense transformers: training FLOP = 6 x parameters x tokens (2 FLOP per parameter per token for the forward pass, about twice that for the backward pass). Example: Llama 3 405B x 15.6 trillion tokens x 6 = 3.79e25 FLOP, matching Meta's reported 3.8e25. For mixture-of-experts models use active rather than total parameters (Qwen3.8-Max: 95B active of 2.4T total).

unit: H100 GPU-hours to train one frontier open model (Llama 3.1 405B, pretraining plus fine-tuning; Meta disclosure)
source: Meta, 'Llama 3.1 Model Card' (llama-models repository, July 2024), training-time table
note: Meta's table gives 30.84M GPU-hours for the 405B model, 7.0M for 70B and 1.46M for 8B, 39.3M in total, on H100-80GB at 700 W TDP; at Lambda's on-demand $3.99 per H100-hour that is about $123 million of rented GPU time for the 405B run (30.84e6 x 3.99), versus Epoch's $50 million amortized-hardware estimate for the same run. Epoch estimates Grok 4 (2025) at 246 million H100-hours, eight times more.

unit: FLOP of training compute realised per H100 GPU-hour (Llama 3 405B: 3.8e25 FLOP over 30.84M GPU-hours)
source: Meta, 'The Llama 3 Herd of Models' (arXiv 2407.21783, 31 Jul 2024), section 1 and section 3.3
note: Arithmetic: 3.8e25 FLOP / 30.84e6 GPU-hours = 1.23e18 FLOP per GPU-hour = 3.4e14 FLOP/s sustained, about 35% of an H100's 9.89e14 FLOP/s dense BF16 peak (model FLOP utilisation), on up to 16,000 H100s. Epoch's Grok 4 inputs (5.0e26 FLOP over 246M H100-hours) imply 2.0e18 per GPU-hour. Use this to turn a GPU-hour budget into a training-compute budget or vice versa.
